evidence.claim: Wooded roads and rolling farmland follow an older trading corridor.
evidence.quote: The narrow roadways travel through tunnels of trees along some stretches and through wide-open farmland along others.

evidence.claim: follow an older trading corridor.
evidence.quote: SR 16 follows the approximate route of an early trail shown on maps from about 1715 to 1755

evidence.claim: The Historic Piedmont Scenic Byway runs through rolling farmland and the Oconee National Forest, crossing the Oconee and Ogeechee rivers.
evidence.quote: the byway travels through the Oconee National Forest, across the Oconee and Ogeechee Rivers, and past acres of rolling farmland.

evidence.claim: Its 82 miles combine State Routes 15, 16 and 77 with rural county roads in Putnam and Hancock counties.
evidence.quote: Traveling through Putnam and Hancock Counties, the Historic Piedmont Scenic Byway stretches for 82 miles, following State Highways 15, 16 and 77, and rural county roads

evidence.claim: Georgia DOT highlights the route’s historic and cultural qualities, from Rock Hawk to antebellum homes.
evidence.quote: From the Rock Hawk effigy, built by Native Americans thousands of years ago, to Glen Mary Plantation and other antebellum homes, this route reveals a region of Georgia that is rich in historic and cultural qualities.

evidence.claim: Narrow roads pass under trees before opening into farmland.
evidence.quote: The narrow roadways travel through tunnels of trees along some stretches and through wide-open farmland along others.

evidence.claim: SR 16 follows the approximate route of the Okfuskee Trail, which connected present-day Augusta with the Mississippi River.
evidence.quote: SR 16 follows the approximate route of an early trail shown on maps from about 1715 to 1755

evidence.claim: Native Americans carried deer pelts along this corridor during the seventeenth century; families from Virginia and the Carolinas later traveled it into the Piedmont.
evidence.quote: Native-Americans carried deer pelts through Putnam and Hancock Counties along the route of today’s Georgia 16.

evidence.claim: The Eatonton Turnpike Company organized to make Eatonton the midpoint of the road between Sparta and Monticello.
evidence.quote: Eatonton Turnpike Company was organized for making Eatonton the midpoint on this road from Sparta to Monticello.

evidence.claim: Travel east from western Putnam County through Willard and Eatonton’s courthouse square, then cross the Oconee into Hancock County.
evidence.quote: continues east through the Oconee National Forest passing over Beaver Creek Dam to the scenic rural farming community of Willard and then over the Little River to Eatonton.

evidence.claim: The main route crosses Shoulderbone Creek and continues through Sparta to Jewell.
evidence.quote: The Shoulderbone Creek bridge is an attractive old bridge dating from the early 20th century, and from it is visible Millmore gristmill, and the Vinson-Harris-Lovejoy house.

evidence.claim: A northern loop and roads toward Linton complete the byway network.
evidence.quote: There are also northern and southern Scenic Byway sections in Hancock County.

evidence.claim: Beyond Jewell, the separate Warren County-Piedmont extension follows SR 16 to Warrenton.
evidence.quote: The Warren County-Piedmont Scenic Byway Extension serves as a continuation of the Historic Piedmont Scenic Byway (located in Putnam and Hancock counties).

evidence.claim: the Okfuskee Trail, which connected present-day Augusta with the Mississippi River.
evidence.quote: The prehistoric trail connected what is now Augusta with the Mississippi River and was know as the Okfuskee Trail

evidence.claim: during the seventeenth century
evidence.quote: In the seventeenth century as the English established the colony of Carolina, Native-Americans carried deer pelts

evidence.claim: families from Virginia and the Carolinas later traveled it into the Piedmont.
evidence.quote: Scores of families from Virginia and the Carolinas moved along the old Indian trail of today’s Georgia Highway 16 as they cleared land in the newly formed counties of the piedmont

evidence.claim: Eatonton’s courthouse square, then cross the Oconee into Hancock County.
evidence.quote: The Byway passes through the Eatonton Historic District and through the scenic courthouse square.

evidence.claim: cross the Oconee into Hancock County.
evidence.quote: crossing the Oconee River into Hancock County, through Sparta to the Hancock/Warren County line at Jewell.

evidence.claim: A northern loop and roads toward Linton complete the byway network.
evidence.quote: Including the SR 16 section this forms a complete loop from Sparta. The southern section begins in Sparta with the intersection of SR 15/16 and Boland Road, travels south to Brown Chapel Road to the second intersection with Linton Road, then goes towards the Linton Community.

evidence.claim: the separate Warren County-Piedmont extension follows SR 16 to Warrenton.
evidence.quote: The Byway traverses eleven miles of gently rolling hills on State Route 16 from the Hancock/Warren County line to the intersection of State Route 12 in the City of Warrenton

evidence.claim: Thousands of quartzite pieces form a large bird at Rock Hawk, but scholars do not know which bird its builders intended.
evidence.quote: It consists of thousands of pieces of quartzite laid in the shape of a large bird. Although it is most often referred to as a hawk, scholars do not know exactly what type of bird the original builders intended to portray.

evidence.claim: The archaeological site lies off SR 16 on Wallace Dam Road, east of Eatonton near Lake Oconee.
evidence.quote: The site is located along Wallace Dam Road, off State Route 16, several miles east of Eatonton, near the shores of the manmade Lake Oconee.

evidence.claim: Rock Eagle, also in Putnam County, is the other known example of this kind of effigy mound east of the Mississippi.
evidence.quote: Only two such effigy mounds have been found east of the Mississippi River. The other, known as Rock Eagle, is also located in Putnam County

evidence.claim: Rock Hawk is in poorer physical condition than Rock Eagle.
evidence.quote: The physical condition of Rock Hawk is far below that of its 'sister' site.

evidence.claim: A tall fence protects the mound itself from entry.
evidence.quote: To protect the site, access to the mound is prohibited, and it is surrounded by a tall fence.

evidence.claim: Shoulderbone Creek joins the Oconee River, and the community of Shoulderbone takes its name from the stream.
evidence.quote: Shoulderbone Creek is a stream in the U.S. state of Georgia. It is a tributary of the Oconee River.

evidence.claim: At the SR 16 crossing, the Historic Piedmont Corridor Management Plan recorded an early-twentieth-century bridge with a view of Millmore gristmill.
evidence.quote: The Shoulderbone Creek bridge is an attractive old bridge dating from the early 20th century, and from it is visible Millmore gristmill, and the Vinson-Harris-Lovejoy house.

evidence.claim: Millmore ground corn and wheat for two centuries.
evidence.quote: The Millmore gristmill at SR 16 and SR 77 in Hancock County turned millstones, grinding corn and wheat for two centuries.

evidence.claim: The same plan documented a treaty marker at the meeting of SR 16 and SR 77, with the Vinson-Harris-Lovejoy house across the road.
evidence.quote: At the junction of these roads, a marker stands to commemorate the Oconee Treaty with Native-Americans. Across the road is the 1820s Vinson-Harris-Lovejoy house, and Millmore gristmill.

evidence.claim: the community of Shoulderbone takes its name from the stream.
evidence.quote: The community was named for its location on Shoulderbone Creek.

evidence.claim: A New England house form appears in Sparta at the Rossiter-Little House: its main section follows a saltbox design.
evidence.quote: The main part of the house is built on a classic New England saltbox design typical of the 17th and 18th centuries.

evidence.claim: Timothy Wells Rossiter, a Revolutionary War surgeon from Connecticut, bought a lot at Broad and Miles Streets.
evidence.quote: Timothy Wells Rossiter, a Revolutionary War surgeon from Connecticut, bought the northeast corner lot at Broad and Miles Streets

evidence.claim: The house departs from that regional pattern with two projecting front wings and a porch between them.
evidence.quote: The Rossiter-Little House has been modified, however, from the archetypical New England form by having two front projecting wings or ells with an inset front porch or gallery between them.

evidence.claim: It belongs to the Sparta Historic District, listed on the National Register in 1974.
evidence.quote: It is a contributing property of the Sparta Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974.

evidence.claim: Sparta became Hancock County’s seat in 1797, two years after its founding.
evidence.quote: Sparta was founded in 1795 in the newly formed Hancock County. It became the county seat in 1797

evidence.claim: The corridor plan describes the principal SR 16 leg and the northern loop as two-lane, two-way roads.
evidence.quote: The second leg, SR 15/SR 77 just north of Sparta, consists of a two-lane, two-way roadway line

evidence.claim: the principal SR 16 leg
evidence.quote: The primary leg, SR 16, extends from western Putnam County to the Warren County line, consists of a two-lane, two- way roadway line

evidence.claim: Later, the byway’s preservation goals joined its historical sites with the surrounding rural landscape.
evidence.quote: The community’s vision is to preserve, enhance and display the history, culture and natural beauty of this rural route

evidence.claim: Scholars have not established whether Rock Hawk suffered more degradation or Rock Eagle received more preservation or reconstruction.
evidence.quote: Scholars do not know if there was greater degradation of the Rock Hawk site, greater preservation or reconstruction at Rock Eagle (which is by far the more famous of the two and a greater 'attraction'), or a combination of these or other factors.

evidence.claim: SR 77 connects this part of SR 16 with SR 15 to form the byway’s northern loop, through wooded land with few visible residences.
evidence.quote: State Route 77 in Hancock County - connects SR 16 to SR 15 to form a loop. This road is bordered on both sides by wooded land, with few visible residences.

evidence.claim: The present building incorporates an older log cabin, whose foundation remains beneath the crawlspace.
evidence.quote: The present structure was built onto and around a log cabin (1797).

evidence.claim: whose foundation remains beneath the crawlspace.
evidence.quote: Beneath the crawlspace of the present house, the original structure of the log foundation is still in place.

evidence.claim: Wooded stretches alternate with open farmland along the narrow roads.
evidence.quote: The narrow roadways travel through tunnels of trees along some stretches and through wide-open farmland along others.

flags: Used Georgia DOT’s 82-mile total, which includes branches; the catalog’s 58.9 mapped miles cover a different itinerary. The old corridor plan also says 85 miles in its transportation section. Warrenton belongs to a separately named extension.

Road/trail distinction retained with the source’s “approximate route” qualification. The corridor plan has apparent chronology errors elsewhere, including county development centuries and a confused Linton Stephens identification; those claims are excluded.

Rock Hawk dating conflicts: 30.txt suggests 1,000–3,000 years and Woodland builders; the corridor plan says thought over 6,000 years. Omitted age and cultural assignment. No tribal or archaeological primary source is cached.

Shoulderbone’s bridge, mill view and marker are described historically because the corridor plan is from the early 2000s. Current structure condition and roadside stopping arrangements are not confirmed. The kept coordinate points to Shoulderbone community, retained as required.

Omitted the current treaty-cession summary: only the old corridor plan supplies it, without treaty text or a Creek source establishing legal scope. Omitted Sparta’s “completely unscathed” claim and reported Culver intervention, supported only by an uncorroborated encyclopedia account.

No current landmark was dropped. Dairy history is supported but omitted for focus; Rock Hawk’s dismissive invitation to imagine a hawk was replaced with the documented uncertainty about bird identification.
